claim: Spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to disturbed sensory, autonomic, and motor functions.
source: Spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to disturbed sensory, autonomic, and motor functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about SCI effects, supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: In the immediate phase following SCI the excitability of the spinal networks caudal to the injury is completely depressed.
source: In the immediate phase following SCI the excitability of the spinal networks caudal to the injury is completely depressed (Klussmann and Martin-Villalba, 2005; Rossignol et al., 2007; Schwab et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The initial state of motor depression after SCI is often followed by a maladaptive state of hyper-excitability of the spinal circuitries referred to as spasticity.
source: This initial state of motor depression is often followed by a maladaptive state of hyper-excitability of the spinal circuitries referred to as spasticity (Biering-Sørensen et al., 2006; Dietz, 2010; Frigon and Rossignol, 2006; Hultborn, 2003; Little et al., 1999; Nielsen et al., 1995, 2007)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Spasticity is characterized by an increase in spinal reflexes and by the appearance of involuntary sustained muscle contractions or spasms.
source: This initial state of motor depression is often followed by a maladaptive state of hyper-excitability of the spinal circuitries referred to as spasticity (Biering-Sørensen et al., 2006; Dietz, 2010; Frigon and Rossignol, 2006; Hultborn, 2003; Little et al., 1999; Nielsen et al., 1995, 2007) and characterized by an increase in spinal reflexes and by the appearance of involuntary sustained muscle contractions or spasms (Nielsen et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spasms are often triggered by innocuous sensory stimuli or muscle stretch.
source: and characterized by an increase in spinal reflexes and by the appearance of involuntary sustained muscle contractions or spasms (Nielsen et al., 2007) often triggered by innocuous sensory stimuli or muscle stretch.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Appearance of spasms has been hypothesized to be related to an increased gain in sensory signaling to motor neurons caused by a reduced pre-synaptic inhibition of sensory afferents.
source: At the premotor neuron level appearance of spasms has been hypothesized to be related to an increased gain in sensory signaling to motor neurons caused by a reduced pre-synaptic inhibition of sensory afferents (Faist et al., 1994; Xia and Rymer, 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Appearance of spasms has been hypothesized to be related to an alteration in the efficacy of spinal inhibitory circuits.
source: At the premotor neuron level appearance of spasms has been hypothesized to be related to an increased gain in sensory signaling to motor neurons caused by a reduced pre-synaptic inhibition of sensory afferents (Faist et al., 1994; Xia and Rymer, 2005), an alteration in the efficacy of spinal inhibitory circuits (Crone et al., 1994, 2004; Pierrot-Deseilligny et al., 1979; Shefner et al., 1992)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Appearance of spasms has been hypothesized to be related to a shift from a hyperpolarizing to a depolarizing action of the inhibitory synaptic inputs onto motor neurons.
source: At the premotor neuron level appearance of spasms has been hypothesized to be related to an increased gain in sensory signaling to motor neurons caused by a reduced pre-synaptic inhibition of sensory afferents (Faist et al., 1994; Xia and Rymer, 2005), an alteration in the efficacy of spinal inhibitory circuits (Crone et al., 1994, 2004; Pierrot-Deseilligny et al., 1979; Shefner et al., 1992), or a shift from a hyperpolarizing to a depolarizing action of the inhibitory synaptic inputs onto motor neurons (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The development of spasms has been linked to the increased expression of plateau potentials in motor neurons.
source: At the motor neuron level the development of spasms has been linked to the increased expression of plateau potentials – carried by voltage-gated persistent Ca2+ and Na+ currents – allowing motor neurons to sustain tonic firing (Bennett et al., 1999; Eken et al., 1989; Kiehn and Eken, 1998; Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004a; Murray et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Plateau potentials are carried by voltage-gated persistent Ca2+ and Na+ currents.
source: At the motor neuron level the development of spasms has been linked to the increased expression of plateau potentials – carried by voltage-gated persistent Ca2+ and Na+ currents – allowing motor neurons to sustain tonic firing (Bennett et al., 1999; Eken et al., 1989; Kiehn and Eken, 1998; Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004a; Murray et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Plateau potentials allow motor neurons to sustain tonic firing.
source: At the motor neuron level the development of spasms has been linked to the increased expression of plateau potentials – carried by voltage-gated persistent Ca2+ and Na+ currents – allowing motor neurons to sustain tonic firing (Bennett et al., 1999; Eken et al., 1989; Kiehn and Eken, 1998; Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004a; Murray et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: All behaviorally relevant motor activities require excitatory drive to orchestrate the generation, maintenance and termination of motor responses.
source: However, all behaviorally relevant motor activities require excitatory drive to orchestrate the generation, maintenance and termination of motor responses (Hägglund et al., 2010; Kiehn, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Muscle spasms may be the result of aberrant spinal excitatory drive to motor neurons.
source: However, all behaviorally relevant motor activities require excitatory drive to orchestrate the generation, maintenance and termination of motor responses (Hägglund et al., 2010; Kiehn, 2016), leading to the possibility that muscle spasms may be the result of aberrant spinal excitatory drive to motor neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on cited research about motor control.

claim: Long-lasting excitatory postsynaptic potentials may be detected in motor neurons during sustained motor responses in chronic spinalized animals.
source: Indeed long-lasting excitatory postsynaptic potentials may be detected in motor neurons during sustained motor responses in chronic spinalized animals (Akay et al., 2014; Brumovsky, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Whether activity in interneurons is involved in initiating, maintaining, and terminating spasms is unknown.
source: Nevertheless, whether activity in interneurons is involved in initiating, maintaining, and terminating spasms is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: A chronic spinal cord mouse model was developed that mimics aspects of SCI.
source: To address these issues we have developed a chronic spinal cord mouse model that mimics aspects of SCI and offers the possibility to combine detailed electrophysiological and imaging studies of both motor neurons and neurotransmitter-defined populations of interneurons to directly monitor and perturb their activity during muscle spasms.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: The chronic spinal cord model was developed in the rat targeting a transection to the sacral segment of the spinal cord.
source: The approach builds on a chronic spinal cord model developed in the rat (Bennett et al., 1999) that targets a transection to the sacral segment of the spinal cord thereby producing spasms in the tail muscles without affecting limb muscles or bowel and bladder functions.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The rat chronic spinal cord model produces spasms in the tail muscles without affecting limb muscles or bowel and bladder functions.
source: The approach builds on a chronic spinal cord model developed in the rat (Bennett et al., 1999) that targets a transection to the sacral segment of the spinal cord thereby producing spasms in the tail muscles without affecting limb muscles or bowel and bladder functions.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: An increased but graded expression of plateau potentials in motor neurons was found, which alone does not account for spontaneous and sensory-evoked spasms.
source: We find an increased but graded expression of plateau potentials in motor neurons, which alone does not account for spontaneous and sensory-evoked spasms.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Optical imaging in chronically spinal cord transected mice unmasked persistent neural activity in spinal interneurons with distinct spatiotemporal relationship during muscle spasms.
source: However, optical imaging in chronically spinal cord transected mice unmasked persistent neural activity in spinal interneurons with distinct spatiotemporal relationship during muscle spasms.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Optogenetic activation and inactivation of spinal excitatory interneurons causally linked their activity to the triggering and maintenance of the spasms.
source: Optogenetic activation and inactivation of spinal excitatory interneurons causally linked their activity to the triggering and maintenance of the spasms.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of spinal inhibitory interneurons revealed a functional inhibition that played a role in sculpturing and curtailing muscle spasms.
source: In contrast, optogenetic stimulation of spinal inhibitory interneurons revealed a functional inhibition that played a role in sculpturing and curtailing muscle spasms.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The study reveals a hitherto unrecognized mechanism for muscle spasms after chronic spinal cord transection whereby assemblies of excitatory interneurons are recruited into functional circuits by weak sensory inputs.
source: Our study reveals a hitherto unrecognized mechanism for muscle spasms after chronic spinal cord transection whereby assemblies of excitatory interneurons are recruited into functional circuits by weak sensory inputs, generating persistent excitatory activity that drives motor neurons even if inhibition is still functionally active.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Assemblies of excitatory interneurons generate persistent excitatory activity that drives motor neurons even if inhibition is still functionally active.
source: Our study reveals a hitherto unrecognized mechanism for muscle spasms after chronic spinal cord transection whereby assemblies of excitatory interneurons are recruited into functional circuits by weak sensory inputs, generating persistent excitatory activity that drives motor neurons even if inhibition is still functionally active.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The study shifts the widely held view that muscle spasms after SCI are the result of increased motor neuron excitability and reduced spinal inhibition acting as a source of excitation.
source: Accordingly, our study shifts the widely held view that muscle spasms after SCI are the result of increased motor neuron excitability and reduced spinal inhibition acting as a source of excitation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The study provides new directions for treatment of spasms after SCI.
source: It therefore provides new directions for treatment of spasms after SCI.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Spasticity developed gradually in the tail after chronic spinal cord transection, plateauing eight weeks after transection.
source: Spasticity developed gradually in the tail, plateauing eight weeks after transection and a chronic change with a typical phenotypical hook-shape appeared in tail posture (bottom panel in Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: A chronic change with a typical phenotypical hook-shape appeared in tail posture after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: Spasticity developed gradually in the tail, plateauing eight weeks after transection and a chronic change with a typical phenotypical hook-shape appeared in tail posture (bottom panel in Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: Spontaneous muscle spasms slowly emerged after chronic spinal cord transection, leading to an increased and prolonged bending of the tail.
source: Spontaneous muscle spasms slowly emerged, leading to an increased and prolonged bending of the tail (Figure 1B and Video 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: A spasm was preceded by low or no motor unit activity.
source: Usually a spasm was preceded by low or no motor unit activity (grey box, Figure 1D)
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: A spasm was initiated by an abrupt activation of several motor units in different segments of the tail.
source: Usually a spasm was preceded by low or no motor unit activity (grey box, Figure 1D) and initiated by an abrupt activation of several motor units in different segments of the tail (green box, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: The massive muscle contraction during a spasm could last up to several minutes before it was slowly released.
source: The massive muscle contraction could last up to several minutes before it was slowly released (violet box Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: Spontaneous spasms occurred on a regular base in the chronic phase after spinal cord transection.
source: Spontaneous spasms occurred on a regular base in the chronic phase after spinal cord transection (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: There was a main rostro-caudal recruitment of the motor units during spasms.
source: Spontaneous spasms occurred on a regular base in the chronic phase after spinal cord transection (Figure 1E) with a main rostro-caudal recruitment of the motor units (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and figure data.

claim: Caudo-rostral recruitment of the motor units may also appear during spasms.
source: with a main rostro-caudal recruitment of the motor units (Figure 1F), even though caudo-rostral recruitment of the motor units may also appear.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations.

claim: Gentle stroking of the tail skin could initiate prolonged spasms similar to those spontaneously evoked.
source: Gentle stroking of the tail skin (Video 2), presumably activating low threshold mechanoceptors or stretch-activated muscle spindles, could initiate prolonged spasms similar to those spontaneously evoked
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations and video data.

claim: Gentle stroking of the tail skin presumably activates low threshold mechanoceptors or stretch-activated muscle spindles.
source: Gentle stroking of the tail skin (Video 2), presumably activating low threshold mechanoceptors or stretch-activated muscle spindles, could initiate prolonged spasms similar to those spontaneously evoked
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge of sensory physiology.

claim: Pronounced triggers for spasms are sensory stimuli.
source: demonstrating that pronounced triggers for spasms are sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: Low intensity electrical stimulation of the tail nerves could evoke prolonged spasms.
source: Similarly, low intensity electrical stimulation of the tail nerves could evoke prolonged spasms (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations.

claim: The chronic sacral transection in adult mouse provides a valid model for studies of spasm development after SCI.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the chronic sacral transection in adult mouse provides a valid model for studies of spasm development after SCI.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: There was a decreased threshold for the monosynaptic activation of motor neurons by low threshold afferents after the chronic transection as compared to acute transection.
source: We found a decreased threshold for the monosynaptic activation of motor neurons by low threshold afferents after the chronic transection as compared to acute transection (defined as control, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting increased motor neuron excitability.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The decreased threshold for monosynaptic activation of motor neurons suggests increased motor neuron excitability.
source: We found a decreased threshold for the monosynaptic activation of motor neurons by low threshold afferents after the chronic transection as compared to acute transection (defined as control, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting increased motor neuron excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: Prolonged muscle activity could be induced by electrical stimulation subthreshold for the monosynaptic activation of motor neurons.
source: Moreover, prolonged muscle activity could be induced by electrical stimulation subthreshold for the monosynaptic activation of motor neurons (the H-reflex) with a different time course from high-threshold stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: With low-threshold stimulation there was a delay in spasm's development with a silent period between the time of stimulation and the prolonged motor response.
source: Typically, with low-threshold stimulation there was a delay in spasm's development with a silent period between the time of stimulation and the prolonged motor response (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The delayed development of the spasm with low-threshold stimulation shows that spasms can be triggered without a direct monosynaptic input onto motor neurons from sensory afferents.
source: The delayed development of the spasm with low-threshold stimulation shows that spasms can be triggered without a direct monosynaptic input onto motor neurons from sensory afferents, pointing to involvement of spinal interneurons in spasm generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: The delayed development of the spasm with low-threshold stimulation points to involvement of spinal interneurons in spasm generation.
source: The delayed development of the spasm with low-threshold stimulation shows that spasms can be triggered without a direct monosynaptic input onto motor neurons from sensory afferents, pointing to involvement of spinal interneurons in spasm generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Four main phenotypic firing patterns of motor units were identified during spontaneous spasms: long-lasting firing, bimodal firing, high frequency firing, and low frequency firing.
source: We identified four main phenotypic firing patterns (Figure 1G–GI): long-lasting firing with a gradual decrease in instantaneous firing frequency (27 ± 6.3, n = 25, N = 5); a bimodal firing, characterized by an initial phase with a high and unstable instantaneous firing frequency (41.48 ± 13.15 Hz, n = 28, N = 5) followed by a lower and more stable firing frequency (23.85 ± 8.5 Hz); and firing where only high (45.55 ± 13.64, n = 9, N = 5) or low firing frequencies (17.87 ± 2.5 Hz, n = 11, N = 5) were expressed.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: There was no correlation between the different motor unit types and their specific distribution along the rostro-caudal axes of the tail.
source: There was no correlation between the different motor unit types and their specific distribution along the rostro-caudal axes of the tail.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations.

claim: The individual motor unit contributes with variable firing patterns to prolonged spasms.
source: These data show that the individual motor unit contributes with variable firing patterns to prolonged spasms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: The isolated spinal cord of chronically transected mice showed all the characteristics of the in situ conditions, including spontaneous or dorsal root stimulus-induced prolonged motor activity (spasms).
source: The isolated spinal cord of chronically transected mice showed all the characteristics of the in situ conditions, including spontaneous (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) or dorsal root stimulus-induced prolonged motor activity (spasms) mimicking sensory activation in vivo (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D), increased motor neuron and interneuron excitability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplements.

claim: The four phenotypic firing patterns observed in vivo were also found in motor neurons from chronically spinal cord transected mice in vitro.
source: The four phenotypic firing patterns, observed in vivo, were also found in motor neurons from chronically spinal cord transected mice in vitro (Figure 2C–F)
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Motor neurons of spinal cords from acutely transected mice displayed a stereotypic response with no activity after termination of the stimulation.
source: while the motor neurons of spinal cords from acutely transected mice displayed a stereotypic response with no activity after termination of the stimulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Motor neurons with strong plateau properties show prolonged firing on the descending half of the ramp leading to a counter-clockwise hysteresis in the frequency-current relationship (f-I).
source: Typically, motor neurons with strong plateau properties show prolonged firing on the descending half of the ramp leading to a counter-clockwise hysteresis in the frequency-current relationship (f-I) (Hounsgaard et al., 1988)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Motor neurons with strong plateau properties have recruitment threshold that is more positive than the de-recruitment threshold leading to a negative ΔI.
source: Typically, motor neurons with strong plateau properties show prolonged firing on the descending half of the ramp leading to a counter-clockwise hysteresis in the frequency-current relationship (f-I) (Hounsgaard et al., 1988), and recruitment threshold that is more positive than the de-recruitment threshold leading to a negative ΔI (recruitment-de-recruitment current) (Bennett et al., 2001b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Motor neurons with long-lasting discharge induced by dorsal root stimulation showed strong plateau properties with counter-clockwise hysteresis and negative ΔI.
source: Motor neurons with long-lasting discharge induced by dorsal root stimulation showed strong plateau properties with counter-clockwise hysteresis and negative ΔI (−1.5 ± 0.6 nA, mean ± SD, n = 7, N = 8, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Motor neurons with a bimodal firing pattern showed linear f-I plots but asymmetric firing with higher recruitment than de-recruitment thresholds.
source: Motor neurons with a bimodal firing pattern showed linear f-I plots but asymmetric firing with higher recruitment than de-recruitment thresholds (ΔI = −0.6 ± 0.4 nA n = 32, N = 8, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Motor neurons that exhibited short-lasting but high frequency responses displayed a linear or a clockwise hysteresis of the f-I plots with lower recruitment than de-recruitment thresholds.
source: Motor neurons that exhibited short-lasting but high frequency responses displayed a linear or a clockwise hysteresis of the f-I plots with lower recruitment than de-recruitment thresholds (ΔI = 168 ± 60 pA, n = 6, N = 8, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Motor neurons with sustained low frequency response after dorsal root stimulation exhibited intermediate plateau properties.
source: Motor neurons with sustained low frequency response after dorsal root stimulation exhibited intermediate plateau properties (ΔI = −1.1 ± 0.9 nA, n = 6, N = 8, Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Most motor neurons recorded in the isolated spinal cord from time-matched sham operated and acutely spinalized animals displayed no sign of plateau potentials.
source: Most motor neurons recorded in the isolated spinal cord from time-matched sham operated and acutely spinalized animals displayed no sign of plateau potentials (21 out of 25 motor neurons, N = 5).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The chronic spinal cord transection induces changes in motor neuron properties with a bias towards the expression of plateau potentials.
source: The chronic spinal cord transection, therefore, induces changes in motor neuron properties with a bias towards the expression of plateau potentials.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The number of motor neuron expressing full plateau properties that may support sustained firing was only about 10%.
source: However, the number of motor neuron expressing full plateau properties that may support sustained firing was only about 10% (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Most motor neurons expressed partial plateau properties, which may promote but not sustain prolonged firing.
source: Most motor neurons expressed partial plateau properties, which may promote but not sustain prolonged firing.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Motor neuron plateau potentials alone seemed unlikely to account for the orchestrated and sustained motor activity underlying muscle spasms after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: Therefore, while motor neuron plateau potentials may contribute they alone seemed unlikely to account for the orchestrated and sustained motor activity underlying muscle spasms after chronic spinal cord transection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: A sustained barrage of synaptic inputs impinged on motor neurons during muscle spasms when motor neurons were hyperpolarized below their firing threshold.
source: A sustained barrage of synaptic inputs impinged on motor neurons during muscle spasms when motor neurons were hyperpolarized below their firing threshold (to −75 mV, Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The silent period immediately following the termination of the sensory stimulation was dominated by inhibitory post-synaptic potentials.
source: The silent period immediately following the termination of the sensory stimulation was dominated by inhibitory post-synaptic potentials that were outnumbered by massive long-lasting excitatory inputs initiating and sustaining the strong depolarization underlying the spasm (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Massive long-lasting excitatory inputs initiate and sustain the strong depolarization underlying the spasm.
source: The silent period immediately following the termination of the sensory stimulation was dominated by inhibitory post-synaptic potentials that were outnumbered by massive long-lasting excitatory inputs initiating and sustaining the strong depolarization underlying the spasm (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Both the duration of the silent period and the duration of depolarization underlying spasms were modulated by the stimulation intensity.
source: Both the duration of the silent period and the duration of depolarization underlying spasms were modulated by the stimulation intensity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Stronger stimulation strength phase advanced the silent period and enhanced the duration and the amplitude of the spasm.
source: Stronger stimulation strength phase advanced the silent period and enhanced the duration and the amplitude of the spasm.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: When inhibitory glycinergic and Gabaergic transmission was blocked, the silent period preceding the spasm in pre-drug conditions disappeared.
source: When inhibitory glycinergic and Gabaergic transmission was blocked, the silent period preceding the spasm in pre-drug conditions disappeared (Figure 3G), showing that the silent period in motor neurons was the result of activity in premotor inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The silent period in motor neurons was the result of activity in premotor inhibitory interneurons.
source: When inhibitory glycinergic and Gabaergic transmission was blocked, the silent period preceding the spasm in pre-drug conditions disappeared (Figure 3G), showing that the silent period in motor neurons was the result of activity in premotor inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The spasm was completely abolished when mephenesin, a blocker of polysynaptic mostly glutamatergic transmission was applied.
source: In contrast the spasm was completely abolished when mephenesin, a blocker of polysynaptic mostly glutamatergic transmission (Cazalets et al., 1995; Kiehn and Butt, 2003; Lev-Tov and Pinco, 1992) was applied (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The spasms were triggered by polysynaptic glutamatergic pathways, and not from direct afferent inputs to motor neurons.
source: Altogether, these experiments show that the spasms were triggered by polysynaptic glutamatergic pathways, and not from direct afferent inputs to motor neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: In chronically spinal cord transected mice low-threshold stimulation of dorsal roots elicited activity in eINs in the superficial dorsal horn with a peak of activity during the stimulation.
source: In both acutely and chronically transected spinal cords low-threshold stimulation of dorsal roots elicited activity in eINs in the superficial dorsal horn with a peak of activity during the stimulation (Figure 4C–D, Video 3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure and video.

claim: In chronically spinal cord transected mice the initial activity in eINs was followed by a second wave of excitatory activity, greater in intensity and longer in duration.
source: However in chronically spinal cord transected mice the initial activity was followed by a second wave of excitatory activity, greater in intensity and longer in duration. It appeared in the ventro-medial horn of the spinal cord and spread to the dorsal horn, finally peaking 3–4 s after the end of the stimulation (red trace in the lower panel of Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A third wave of excitatory activity appeared again in the deep ventral horn, corresponding to the activity observed in the ventral root recordings.
source: Lastly a third wave of excitatory activity appeared again in the deep ventral horn, corresponding to the activity observed in the ventral root recordings (blue trace in the lower panel of Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A change in activity pattern was also seen in iINs when acutely and chronically spinal cord transected mice were compared.
source: A change in activity pattern was also seen in iINs when acutely and chronically spinal cord transected mice were compared (Video 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the video.

claim: In acutely spinal cord transected mice dorsal root stimulation evoked a short-lasting response of iINs in the dorsal horn.
source: In acutely spinal cord transected mice dorsal root stimulation evoked a short-lasting response of iINs in the dorsal horn (Figure 4F, red trace lower panel).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: In chronically spinal cord transected mice dorsal root stimulation resulted in a greater and sustained activation of iINs whose activity spreads from the dorsal horn to the ventral horn, lasting several seconds.
source: Surprisingly, in chronically spinal cord transected mice the same stimulation resulted in a greater and sustained activation of iINs whose activity spreads from the dorsal horn (red trace in Figure 4G) to the ventral horn, lasting several seconds (blue trace in Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Inhibitory circuits exhibited a greater and sustained activation after chronic spinal cord transection, suggesting their involvement in muscle spasm sculpturing and termination.
source: Thus contrary to expected, inhibitory circuits exhibited a greater and sustained activation after chronic spinal cord transection, suggesting their involvement in muscle spasm sculpturing and termination.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory circuits located both in the dorsal and ventral horns show prolonged activity after a chronic spinal cord transection and their activity is temporally related to the spasms.
source: These experiments show that excitatory and inhibitory circuits located both in the dorsal and ventral horns show prolonged activity after a chronic spinal cord transection and their activity is temporally related to the spasms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: EINs and iINs in chronically spinal cord transected mice exhibited spatially and temporally segregated activity.
source: EINs and iINs in chronically spinal cord transected mice exhibited spatially and temporally segregated activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: In spinal cords of acutely spinal cord transected mice, low-threshold stimulation of the dorsal root generated a sequential activation of eINs with a mean peak of activity during the stimulation period followed by iINs immediately after the end of the stimulation.
source: In spinal cords of acutely spinal cord transected mice, low-threshold stimulation of the dorsal root generated a sequential activation of eINs with a mean peak of activity during the stimulation period (−0.22 ± 0.24, mean ± SD) followed by iINs immediately after the end of the stimulation (0.06 ± 0.13).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: In chronically spinal cord transected mice, a second delayed peak of excitatory activity appeared at the beginning of the spasm and a second peak of inhibitory activity appeared just before the spasm ended.
source: However, in chronically spinal cord transected mice, a second delayed peak of excitatory activity appeared at the beginning of the spasm (1.17 ± 0.2) and a second peak of inhibitory activity appeared just before the spasm ended (1.855 ± 0.25, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The spinal network displays persistent neural activity.
source: These experiments show that the spinal network displays persistent neural activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: In acutely transected mice light stimulation of Vglut2+ cells generated movements of the tail for the duration of stimulation only.
source: In acutely transected mice (0–7 days) light stimulation generated movements of the tail for the duration of stimulation only (black trace in Figure 6B, Video 5; N = 5).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure and video.

claim: In chronically transected mice light stimulation of Vglut2+ cells resulted in a long lasting bending of the tail that lasted several minutes after the end of the stimulation.
source: In contrast, the same stimulation applied to chronically transected mice resulted in a long lasting bending of the tail that lasted several minutes after the end of the stimulation (red trace in Figure 6B and Video 5; N = 7).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure and video.

claim: Similar prolonged firing was evoked in the isolated sacral cord from chronically spinal cord transected mice when any one of the spinal segments was optogenetically stimulated.
source: Similar prolonged firing was evoked in the isolated sacral cord from chronically spinal cord transected mice when any one of the spinal segments was optogenetically stimulated (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The sustained activity lasted even longer when inhibitory transmission was blocked.
source: The sustained activity lasted even longer when inhibitory transmission was blocked.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The sustained activity was almost abolished when glutamatergic neuro-transmission was silenced.
source: In contrast it was almost abolished when glutamatergic neuro-transmission was silenced (Figure 6c), leaving only a small direct activation of MNs, likely due to early expression of Vglut2 in some MNs (Nishimaru et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Light stimulation led to antidromic activation of afferents, but this activation was short-lasting (20–50 ms) and only present in the beginning of the stimulation.
source: These recordings showed that light stimulation indeed led to antidromic activation of afferents, but that this activation was short-lasting (20–50 ms) and only present in the beginning of the stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The dominant effect of light stimulation on spasm generation does not originate from the activation of Vglut2+ afferents.
source: These experiments exclude that the dominant effect of light stimulation on spasm generation originates from the activation of Vglut2+ afferents since neither persistent firing of the Vglut2 terminals nor persistent dorsal root reflexes (Bos et al., 2011) were seen.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Spasm generation was prevented when optogenetic silencing of eINs was simultaneously applied to the same segment as the electrical stimulation.
source: Spasm generation was prevented when optogenetic silencing was simultaneously applied to the same segment as the electrical stimulation (Figure 6DII–III and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-E)
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The monosynaptic inputs to motor neurons were intact during the co-incident electrical and light stimulation.
source: This inhibitory effect was not due to inhibition of neurotransmitter release from all afferents since the monosynaptic inputs to motor neurons were intact during the co-incident electrical and light stimulation (compare insets in Figure 6DII–III)
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The recorded dorsal-root-evoked potentials were reduced by less than 10% during light illumination.
source: This inhibitory effect was not due to inhibition of neurotransmitter release from all afferents since the monosynaptic inputs to motor neurons were intact during the co-incident electrical and light stimulation (compare insets in Figure 6DII–III) and the recorded dorsal-root-evoked potentials were reduced by less than 10% during light illumination (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Activity of intrinsic excitatory neuronal circuits in the spinal cord is necessary and sufficient to trigger and maintain muscle spasms.
source: These experiments show that activity of intrinsic excitatory neuronal circuits in the spinal cord is necessary and sufficient to trigger and maintain muscle spasms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The persistent neural activity is generated and maintained only in chronically but not in the acutely transected animals.
source: The persistent neural activity is generated and maintained only in chronically but not in the acutely transected animals, highlighting the profound differences between the changes underlying spinal circuit reorganization in the chronic as compared to the acute phase of spinal cord transection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Recruitment of inter-segmentally connected Vglut2+ neurons seems an essential network mechanism supporting spasm generation.
source: Recruitment of inter-segmentally connected Vglut2+ neurons seems an essential network mechanism supporting spasm generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of iINs in vivo or in vitro never induced muscle spasms or sustained firing after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of iINs in vivo (n = 5) or in vitro (n = 7) never induced muscle spasms or sustained firing after chronic spinal cord transection (Figure 6EI)
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Activation of inhibitory synapses is not sufficient to excite MNs and initiate muscle spasms even though the chloride reversal potential might be shifted to more positive levels after SCI.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of iINs in vivo (n = 5) or in vitro (n = 7) never induced muscle spasms or sustained firing after chronic spinal cord transection (Figure 6EI), demonstrating that activation of inhibitory synapses is not sufficient to excite MNs and initiate muscle spasms even though the chloride reversal potential might be shifted to more positive levels after SCI (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Optogenetic in vivo activation of iINs in chronically spinal cord transected animals suppressed muscle spasms.
source: Optogenetic in vivo activation of iINs in chronically spinal cord transected animals suppressed muscle spasms (Video 6, N = 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the video.

claim: The motor response suppression by optogenetic activation of iINs was related to the stimulation period and the spasms reappeared as soon as the stimulation terminated.
source: However, the motor response suppression was related to the stimulation period and the spasms reappeared as soon as the stimulation terminated (Video 6).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the video.

claim: When iINs were stimulated during the afferent activation it directly inhibited the synaptic release preventing development of a spasm.
source: When iINs were stimulated during the afferent activation it directly inhibited the synaptic release preventing development of a spasm (Figure 6EII).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: When stimulating iINs during muscle spasms these where prematurely inhibited.
source: When stimulating during muscle spasms these where prematurely inhibited (Figure 6EIII).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Light-induced inhibition of iINs during the pre-motor silent period phases advanced the prolonged motor neuron firing.
source: Lastly, light-induced inhibition of iINs during the pre-motor silent period phases advanced the prolonged motor neuron firing (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: iINs neither generate nor maintain muscle spasms.
source: The in vivo and in vitro experiments showed that iINs neither generate nor maintain muscle spasms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Inhibitory circuits generate functional inhibition onto motor neurons that sculpture the spasms generation by introducing a delay to their onset and participating in their termination.
source: Rather inhibitory circuits generate functional inhibition onto motor neurons that sculpture the spasms generation by introducing a delay to their onset and participating in their termination.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Muscle spasms are generated by a combination of persistent activity in sequentially recruited spinal excitatory interneurons that interact with a graded expression of plateau potentials in motor neurons.
source: Here we demonstrate that muscle spasms are generated by a combination of persistent activity in sequentially recruited spinal excitatory interneurons that interact with a graded expression of plateau potentials in motor neurons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Inhibition is functional active and does not drive the spasms.
source: Moreover, we show that inhibition is functional active and does not drive the spasms.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Several studies reported the appearance of long-lasting EPSPs at the motor neuron level after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: Several studies reported the appearance of long-lasting EPSPs at the motor neuron level after chronic spinal cord transection (Akay et al., 2014; Brumovsky, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The contribution of the excitatory inputs has been neglected as a direct cause of spasms generation and maintenance.
source: Several studies reported the appearance of long-lasting EPSPs at the motor neuron level after chronic spinal cord transection (Akay et al., 2014; Brumovsky, 2013) but the contribution of the excitatory inputs has been neglected as a direct cause of spasms generation and maintenance.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in prior research.

claim: Motor neurons receive a massive barrage of excitatory inputs during spasms.
source: First, motor neurons receive a massive barrage of excitatory inputs during spasms.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The temporal dynamics of the excitatory spinal interneuron activity correspond to the spasm generation.
source: Second, the temporal dynamics of the excitatory spinal interneuron activity correspond to the spasm generation.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Light stimulation In Vglut2Cre; ChR2 mice initiated spasms.
source: Thirdly, light stimulation In Vglut2Cre; ChR2 mice initiated spasms.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The absence or the severe reduction of spasms when eINs were optogenetically inhibited suggested a necessary role of eINs that could not be substituted by direct monosynaptic activation of motor neurons mediated by Vglut1 expression primary afferents.
source: Finally, the absence or the severe reduction of spasms when eINs were optogenetically inhibited suggested a necessary role of eINs that could not be substituted by direct monosynaptic activation of motor neurons mediated by Vglut1 expression primary afferents (Brumovsky, 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The sustained activity was not generated by excitatory persistent dorsal root reflexes.
source: Importantly, the sustained activity was not generated by excitatory persistent dorsal root reflexes (Bos et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The study complements previous studies using a chronic spinal cord transection model of the sacral spinal cord in rats which showed a graded expression of plateau properties in motor neurons below the transection.
source: With respect to motor neurons our study complement previous studies using a chronic spinal cord transection model of the sacral spinal cord in rats which showed a graded expression of plateau properties in motor neurons below the transection (Bennett et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The plateau properties are generated by persistent Ca2+ and Na+ currents.
source: The plateau properties are generated by persistent Ca2+ and Na+ currents (Li and Bennett, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The manifestations of plateau properties are regulated by constitutively opened 5-HT receptors.
source: The plateau properties are generated by persistent Ca2+ and Na+ currents (Li and Bennett, 2003), whose manifestations are regulated by constitutively opened 5-HT receptors (Murray et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The manifestations of plateau properties are regulated by 5-HT released from cells in the spinal cord containing the enzyme aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase.
source: The plateau properties are generated by persistent Ca2+ and Na+ currents (Li and Bennett, 2003), whose manifestations are regulated by constitutively opened 5-HT receptors (Murray et al., 2010) or 5-HT released from cells in the spinal cord containing the enzyme aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (Wienecke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Motor plateau properties are more prevalent after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: Our study also shows that motor plateau properties are more prevalent after chronic spinal cord transection
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The degree of expression of plateau properties matches the firing pattern of individual motor neurons during spasms.
source: Our study also shows that motor plateau properties are more prevalent after chronic spinal cord transection, and the degree of expression of these properties matches the firing pattern of individual motor neurons during spasms.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Only about 10% of the motor neurons express full plateau potentials needed to support sustained firing after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: However, similar to what has been reported in the rat (Bennett et al., 2001b) we find that only about 10% of the motor neurons express full plateau potentials needed to support sustained firing (Hounsgaard et al., 1988; Kiehn et al., 1996) after chronic spinal cord transection.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: The majority of motor neurons expressed partial plateau properties, characterized by membrane properties that will promote but not by themselves sustain prolonged firing in the absence of synaptic inputs.
source: The majority of motor neurons expressed partial plateau properties, characterized by membrane properties that will promote but not by themselves sustain prolonged firing in the absence of synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: These findings underscore the contribution of biophysical properties to prolonged firing in motor neurons after SCI but make it unlikely that motor neuron plateau properties are the main carrier of spasms.
source: Together, these findings underscore the contribution of these biophysical properties to prolonged firing in motor neurons after SCI but make it unlikely that motor neuron plateau properties are the main carrier of spasms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Alteration in inhibitory circuits after SCI has been described in multiple studies as a result of reduced presynaptic inhibition.
source: Alteration in inhibitory circuits after SCI has been described in multiple studies as a result of reduced presynaptic inhibition (Mukherjee and Chakravarty, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Alteration in inhibitory circuits after SCI has been described as a result of reduced reciprocal inhibition.
source: Alteration in inhibitory circuits after SCI has been described in multiple studies as a result of reduced presynaptic inhibition (Mukherjee and Chakravarty, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2007), reduced reciprocal inhibition (Mukherjee and Chakravarty, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Alteration in inhibitory circuits after SCI has been described as a result of down-regulation of the KCC2 chloride-transporter in motor neurons.
source: Alteration in inhibitory circuits after SCI has been described in multiple studies as a result of reduced presynaptic inhibition (Mukherjee and Chakravarty, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2007), reduced reciprocal inhibition (Mukherjee and Chakravarty, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2007) and down-regulation of the KCC2 chloride-transporter in motor neurons (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The findings explicitly demonstrate that the activity of iINs is increased after chronic spinal cord transection with no sign of a decreased efficacy of inhibitory inputs onto motor neurons.
source: In contrast, our findings explicitly demonstrate that the activity of iINs is increased after chronic spinal cord transection with no sign of a decreased efficacy of inhibitory inputs onto motor neurons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The presence of a silent period preceding electrically-evoked spasm suggested that inhibition was still activated by sensory stimulation and it was able to suppress motor neuron responses.
source: The presence of a silent period preceding electrically-evoked spasm suggested that inhibition was still activated by sensory stimulation and it was able to suppress motor neuron responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The optogenetic activation of iINs in the sacral spinal cord was able to suppress spasms and all motor responses after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: Furthermore, the optogenetic activation of iINs in the sacral spinal cord was able to suppress spasms and all motor responses after chronic spinal cord transection.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: iINs were not able to generate and/or maintain the persistent neural activity driving MNs during muscle spasms.
source: In contrast, iINs were not able to generate and/or maintain the persistent neural activity driving MNs during muscle spasms as revealed by optogenetic stimulation both in vivo and in vitro
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Inhibition is not reverted to depolarizing IPSPs that triggers motor output.
source: In contrast, iINs were not able to generate and/or maintain the persistent neural activity driving MNs during muscle spasms as revealed by optogenetic stimulation both in vivo and in vitro, showing that inhibition is not reverted to depolarizing IPSPs that triggers motor output.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The functional role of inhibition is to sculpture and terminate the prolonged spasms.
source: So the functional role of inhibition is to sculpture and terminate the prolonged spasms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The study shifts the focus away from a decreased inhibition as a cause of spasm generation and reassigns to iINs a key functional role in shaping the temporal expression of muscle spasms and its termination.
source: Our study therefore shifts the focus away from a decreased inhibition as a cause of spasm generation and reassigns to iINs a key functional role in shaping the temporal expression of muscle spasms and its termination.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Profound changes at the network as well as at the single cell level appear in the chronic state of SCI in humans as well as in animal models.
source: Profound changes at the network as well as at the single cell level appear in the chronic state of SCI in humans as well as in animal models (Maier and Schwab, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The study represents the first investigation where the functional impact of changes after chronic SCI has been directly tested.
source: Our study represents the first investigation where the functional impact of these changes has been directly tested, revealing insights about the operational logic of spinal circuits after injury.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The appearance of persistent activity in spinal circuits may emerge from changes in network properties and/or biophysical properties of the spinal INs after transection.
source: The appearance of persistent activity in spinal circuits may emerge from changes in network properties and/or biophysical properties of the spinal INs after transection.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about mechanisms.

claim: The number of cells responding to low-threshold dorsal root stimulation appeared to be much higher after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: Indeed, the number of cells responding to low-threshold dorsal root stimulation appeared to be much higher after chronic spinal cord transection.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental observations.

claim: Proprioceptive afferents provide stronger activation of excitatory neurons due to intraspinal sprouting of proprioceptive afferents.
source: Possible explanations for this are that proprioceptive afferents – whose activity is important for motor recovery after spinal cord transection (Akay et al., 2014; Takeoka et al., 2014) – provide stronger activation of excitatory neurons due to intraspinal sprouting of proprioceptive afferents (Krenz and Weaver, 1998)
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Proprioceptive afferents provide stronger activation of excitatory neurons due to reduced presynaptic inhibition.
source: Possible explanations for this are that proprioceptive afferents – whose activity is important for motor recovery after spinal cord transection (Akay et al., 2014; Takeoka et al., 2014) – provide stronger activation of excitatory neurons due to intraspinal sprouting of proprioceptive afferents (Krenz and Weaver, 1998) or due to reduced presynaptic inhibition (Kathe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: The increased activity of excitatory interneurons may engage mechanisms of feed-forward and/or recurrent excitation.
source: The increased activity of excitatory interneurons may also engage mechanisms of feed-forward and/or recurrent excitation (Abbinanti et al., 2012; Wang, 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Feed-forward circuits among excitatory neurons may be recruited by the chronic spinal cord transection as a result of intraspinal sprouting.
source: Feed-forward circuits among excitatory neurons may be recruited by the chronic spinal cord transection as a result of intraspinal sprouting.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation.

claim: Recurrent excitatory loops may develop or be released after the transection.
source: Moreover, since the populations of eINs were activated more than once, recurrent excitatory loops may develop or be released after the transection.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on observations.

claim: Plateau potentials or voltage dependent amplification due to the presence of persistent inward currents in interneurons is also likely to be involved.
source: Finally, plateau potentials or voltage dependent amplification due to the presence of persistent inward currents in interneurons is also likely to be involved.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation.

claim: Interneurons in dorsal and ventral horns may express plateau properties before and after chronic spinal cord transection.
source: Previous experiments have shown that interneurons in dorsal and ventral horns may express plateau properties before (Abbinanti et al., 2012; Derjean et al., 2003; Russo and Hounsgaard, 1994; Theiss et al., 2007) and after chronic spinal cord transection (Dougherty and Hochman, 2008; Husch et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The clinical treatment of spasms relies mostly on drugs acting on GABA receptors suppressing motor responses at the premotor neuronal level.
source: The clinical treatment of spasms relies mostly on drugs acting on GABA receptors suppressing motor responses at the premotor neuronal level (Dietz, 2010; Li et al., 2004b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The nature of the changes underlying chronic spinal cord transection opens up new understandings and potential new targets in treating the maladaptive state of spinal circuits after SCI.
source: The nature of the changes underlying chronic spinal cord transection, we described here, opens up new understandings and potential new targets in treating the maladaptive state of spinal circuits after SCI.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Some of the most promising pharmacological approaches for the therapeutic management of traumatic SCI seem to exert their main motor effect through a silencing of glutamatergic transmission, like riluzole.
source: Some of the most promising pharmacological approaches for the therapeutic management of traumatic SCI seem to exert their main motor effect through a silencing of glutamatergic transmission, like riluzole (Krenz and Weaver, 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Some of the most promising pharmacological approaches for the therapeutic management of traumatic SCI seem to exert their main motor effect through a silencing of glutamatergic transmission, like the different blockers of the serotonin receptors.
source: Some of the most promising pharmacological approaches for the therapeutic management of traumatic SCI seem to exert their main motor effect through a silencing of glutamatergic transmission, like riluzole (Krenz and Weaver, 1998), and the different blockers of the serotonin receptors (Murray et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Selective interference with glutamatergic transmission could open the possibility to dampen the persistent activity in excitatory circuits, leaving the inhibitory ones intact.
source: Indeed selective interference with glutamatergic transmission could open the possibility to dampen the persistent activity in excitatory circuits, leaving the inhibitory ones intact, as obtained with drugs currently used for antiepileptic treatment and off target for chronic pain treatment (Landmark, 2007; Sills, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential treatments supported by citations.
